22 23 --- 24 25 ## Contents 26 27 1. [The short version](#the-short-version) 28 2. [The problem](#the-problem) 29 3. [What LaunchWitness does](#what-launchwitness-does) 30 4. [Try it in two minutes (for judges)](#try-it-in-two-minutes-for-judges) 31 5. [The seller's journey, step by step](#the-sellers-journey-step-by-step) 32 6. [What "proven" means](#what-proven-means) 33 7. [The Doctor: fixing what breaks](#the-doctor-fixing-what-breaks) 34 8. [Keeping watch after launch](#keeping-watch-after-launch) 35 9. [The shop itself](#the-shop-itself) 36 10. [Safety: why an AI can be trusted with this](#safety-why-an-ai-can-be-trusted-with-this) 37 11. [How GoDaddy is used](#how-godaddy-is-used) 38 12. [How Claude is used](#how-claude-is-used) 39 13. [Architecture](#architecture) 40 14. [Tech stack](#tech-stack) 41 15. [Repository layout](#repository-layout) 42 16. [Running it yourself](#running-it-yourself) 43 17. [Testing](#testing) 44 18. [Security](#security) 45 19. [What's real today, and what isn't yet](#whats-real-today-and-what-isnt-yet) 46 20. [How it was built](#how-it-was-built) 47 21. [What's next](#whats-next) 48 22. [Further reading](#further-reading) 49 50 --- 51 52 ## The short version 53 54 Lots of tools will build a small business a website. Almost none of them tell the owner whether a customer's order will actually reach them. 55 56 **LaunchWitness is a website builder that doesn't stop at "your site is ready".** A home seller types a few lines about their business and pastes their price list (or uploads a photo of it). LaunchWitness then: 57 58 1. **Builds** a mobile-friendly shop with their menu, prices, order form, WhatsApp button and UPI payment for each order. 59 2. **Puts it online** on GoDaddy: the web address, the DNS settings, HTTPS and email. 60 3. **Proves it works** by placing a real test order through the real order form and following it all the way to the inbox. 61 4. **Fixes what breaks** using a small, fixed list of safe repairs, and explains every problem in one plain sentence. 62 5. **Keeps checking** after launch, and emails the owner before something breaks or expires. 63 64 The report only says **"Your business is ready for customers."** when every one of those checks has passed, and every claim on it is backed by stored, tamper-evident evidence. 65 66 --- 67 68 ## The problem 69 70 Meet **Meera** (our demo persona). She bakes eggless cakes at home in Pune. Customers find her on Instagram and order in direct messages. She has no website, no business email, and "DNS" means nothing to her. 71 72 Sellers like Meera run into three problems: 73 74 | Problem | What it looks like | 75 |---|---| 76 | **Setup is technical.** | Domains, DNS records, certificates and email settings are a foreign language. Many small sellers never get online at all, and many of those who plan to want someone else to do it for them. | 77 | **Half-working setups go unnoticed.** | A missing email setting means order emails land in spam. Studies of small-business domains repeatedly find missing SPF and DMARC records (a March 2026 analysis put DMARC adoption at about 45% for small businesses, against about 75% for large ones). The owner doesn't see an error message. They just think business is slow. | 78 | **AI could do the setup, but isn't trusted to.** | Setting up a business online means spending money and changing settings. An owner who can't read a DNS record can't check an AI's work. | 79 80 LaunchWitness answers all three: it does the technical work, it **proves** the result instead of assuming it, and it is built so the AI can never spend money or change settings on its own. 81 82 --- 83 84 ## What LaunchWitness does 85 86 In order of importance: 87 88 1. **Proof.** Before the owner shares their link with a single customer, a real test order has to travel through their public order form and arrive. LaunchWitness also checks that the address points to the right place, that the site opens securely, and that the email settings are right. Each step is recorded with the time and the server that answered. 89 2. **Repair (the Doctor).** A failed check is explained in one sentence a non-technical person understands ("Order emails could land in spam: a protection setting is missing"), repaired from a fixed list of five safe fixes, and checked again. Nothing outside that list can ever run. 90 3. **Watching.** After launch, the site is re-checked every 15 minutes and the settings daily. The owner is emailed at their personal address (not the business inbox, which might be the thing that's broken). 91 4. **Building, last.** If the seller has no site yet, LaunchWitness builds one from what they typed, in one of six looks designed for home businesses (bakery, home kitchen, handmade, tailoring, gifts, general). 92 93 Building is listed last on purpose. Plenty of products build sites. The new part is the proof. 94 95 --- 96 97 ## Try it in two minutes (for judges) 98 99 No account, no payment, nothing to install: 100 101 1. Open **https://launchwitness.com** and press **Try it**. 102 2. Pick one of the example sellers (or type your own description and price list). 103 3. Review the shop it built, choose a look, and run a **practice launch**. Practice mode runs every step against a pretend GoDaddy, so nothing is bought and nothing goes on the internet. It is always clearly labelled "Practice". 104 4. Watch the checks run, then open the report. 105 106 To see a **real** launch that has already happened: 107 108 - **Live shop:** https://meeras-eggless-bakes.launchwitness.com (its DNS record was written by the app through the GoDaddy API; its HTTPS certificate was issued on demand by Let's Encrypt). 109 - **Its shared proof report:** https://launchwitness.com/r/GsZj7gOAoCydSauqdNpoaWksKHVW-HSz. Press **Verify** to recompute the evidence chain yourself. 110 111 Other things worth a look: 112 113 - **Check any address** on the landing page (`/#check`): type any domain and get a plain-English health check of its address, HTTPS certificate and email settings. 114 - **Demo shops:** `/demo/meera`, `/demo/imran`, `/demo/sunita`. 115 - **Sign in** with any email address to see the account side. New accounts can practise straight away; real launches need the team's approval during the beta. 116 117 --- 118 119 ## The seller's journey, step by step 120 121 | # | Step | Who does it | What happens | 122 |---|---|---|---| 123 | 1 | **Describe** | Seller + Claude | The seller types a few lines and pastes a price list or uploads a photo of one (even handwritten). One Claude call reads it into a structured profile: business name, products and prices in ₹, hours, area, pickup or delivery, notice needed, UPI name, food licence number if given, plus the shop's wording and look. If the business takes **bookings** rather than orders (a salon, a tutor), it says so plainly and doesn't build a half-working shop. | 124 | 2 | **Review** | Seller | The profile appears as an ordinary form. The seller fixes anything wrong, adds photos, picks one of six looks and an accent colour, and sees a private live preview. No AI involved. | 125 | 3 | **Pick a name** | Claude + code | Claude suggests about ten names. Code checks which are really available and what they cost, and shows the best three. (Today, real launches use a free `.launchwitness.com` address.) | 126 | 4 | **Approve** | Seller | One card shows every step, every setting as **before → after**, and the exact cost. **Nothing is bought or changed until the seller taps Approve.** | 127 | 5 | **Launch** | Code only | Back up the current DNS settings, point the address at the server, set up email, turn the site on with HTTPS. Each step streams on screen and is logged. | 128 | 6 | **Prove** | Code (+ Claude to explain) | Run every check, including a real test order. Anything that fails goes to the Doctor, gets a safe fix, and is checked again. | 129 | 7 | **Report and watch** | Code | A report with every check, its result and time, the Doctor's explanations, and the full audit log. A shareable read-only link. Monitoring starts. | 130 131 After launch the seller also gets an **Orders** page (New → Confirmed → Paid → Done / Cancelled, with a one-tap WhatsApp message to the customer, and a "Customer says paid" note when a customer sends their UPI reference), new-order emails at their personal address, and an account page where they can delete everything. 132 133 --- 134 135 ## What "proven" means 136 137 Most tools would call a site "live" once the page loads. LaunchWitness is stricter. Each claim on the report comes from a stored `Evidence` row, and each hop is recorded separately: 138 139 | Check | How it's proven | Why it's done this way | 140 |---|---|---| 141 | **The address leads to the shop** | Asked of the domain's **own authoritative nameservers** (found from its NS records), not a cached resolver. The answering server is recorded. Google, Cloudflare and Quad9 are also asked, as information only. | Cached resolvers can show old answers for hours. The authoritative answer is the truth. | 142 | **The shop opens securely** | An HTTPS request with full certificate validation, **and** the page must carry the shop's own `` marker. | A parked page with a valid certificate would otherwise pass. | 143 | **Email settings are right** | MX, SPF, DKIM and DMARC are looked up. The email provider is recognised from the domain's mail servers, and advice only ever uses that provider's values. | A missing setting silently sends orders to spam. | 144 | **A real order arrives** | The checker opens the public shop page, finds the order form and submits it exactly like a customer would (same fields, same form token), carrying a one-time code. Then it records: *form accepted* → *mail server accepted* (with message id) → *in the inbox* (read over IMAP, for mailboxes the app holds) **or** *owner confirmed* (a single-use "Yes, I got it" link inside the test email). | This is the whole point: the path a customer's order takes, tested end to end. | 145 | **The launch finished cleanly** | The step log shows every step done. | A half-finished launch can be resumed or undone. | 146 147 Two rules keep the report honest: 148 149 - **"Accepted" is never shown as "delivered".** Until the order is seen in the inbox or the owner confirms it, the report says something like "6 of 7 proven, 1 needs you" and the headline is "Almost ready". 150 - **"Not sure" is allowed. A wrong answer is not.** Every finding says how sure it is: *seen*, *not seen*, or *couldn't check*. If a lookup fails on our side, that is "couldn't check": never a pass, never the seller's fault, never an alert. 151 152 **The evidence is tamper-evident.** Each shop's evidence rows form an append-only hash chain (`app/chain.py`), written only through one function (`proof.add`). Anyone with the shared report link can press **Verify** (or call `GET /r//verify`), and the server recomputes the chain and says either "Intact" or exactly which saved step changed. 153 154 --- 155 156 ## The Doctor: fixing what breaks 157 158 Launches go wrong in ordinary ways: settings that haven't spread yet, a certificate that fails first time, a mailbox that isn't ready, a step that stops halfway. The Doctor handles these. 159 160 **How it works:** 161 162 1. A check fails. 163 2. For an address, padlock or test-order failure, the Doctor (Claude, cheap model) may first **investigate** using five **read-only** tools: `resolve` (the shop's own address), `fetch` (the shop's own page, through the SSRF guard), `evidence` (the stored proof of this run), `smtp_test` (connect and sign in to the mail server, never send) and `mailbox_status`. It gets at most 4 looks. 164 3. It answers with a finding in one plain sentence and **either** a fix id from the playbook **or** "needs you" with plain instructions for the owner. 165 4. **Code** checks the answer and is the only thing that acts. 166 167 **The playbook is five fixes, fixed in code** (`backend/app/agents/playbook.py`): 168 169 | Fix | What it does | 170 |---|---| 171 | `restore_backup` | Put every setting this launch touched back exactly as it was before (undo). Needs the owner. | 172 | `readd_mx` | Re-add the mail-server setting from the approved plan. | 173 | `readd_email_auth` | Re-add the SPF / DKIM / DMARC settings from the approved plan. | 174 | `retry_certificate` | Ask for the HTTPS certificate again. | 175 | `repoint_site` | Point the address at the shop again. | 176 177 **Limits:** at most 3 attempts per check, no fix ever spends money, and every attempt is written to the audit log. A fix the model suggests that isn't in the playbook, or isn't allowed for that check and launch type, is refused and logged. If Claude is unavailable or over budget, plain rules decide instead: if exactly one fix is allowed it is applied and labelled "Standard fix", otherwise the owner gets clear instructions. 178 179 On the report, each investigation is shown as a short timeline: *Looked up where your address leads → it leads nowhere → Pointed your address at your shop again → Checked again: working.* 180 181 **Describe the problem:** an owner can also type what they or a customer saw ("my customer says the page won't open"). Every check runs again and their words go to the Doctor, fenced off as data so they can't be used as instructions. 182 183 --- 184 185 ## Keeping watch after launch 186 187 GoDaddy's APIs have no webhooks, so LaunchWitness re-runs its checks on a timer: 188 189 | How often | What is checked | 190 |---|---| 191 | **Every 15 minutes** | The site opens, HTTPS is valid, the shop marker is present. | 192 | **Daily** | Address and email settings still match the launch; days left on the certificate and domain; a fresh test order, sent to LaunchWitness's own check mailbox (never to the owner) and found there over IMAP; answers from three public resolvers. | 193 | **On demand** | "Run checks now" on the report. | 194 195 Rules it follows: 196 197 - **A seller only gets a test email when she asked for one** (at launch, "Run checks now" or "Describe the problem"). Every test email's subject starts with `TEST, not a real order:` and opens with a grey "This is a check" banner, with no customer call or WhatsApp buttons. Test orders never appear on the Orders page or count against her daily limit. 198 - A failure is re-checked a minute later to rule out a blip before anything happens. 199 - Something that needs money or the owner's action (a renewal) is an **alert only**, sent 30, 7 and 1 days ahead. 200 - A check that has been fixed 3 times in a day and breaks again is no longer fixed automatically. The owner gets one "keeps breaking" email. 201 - Alerts go to the owner's **personal email**, through an outbox that saves every email first and retries with growing waits, so an order is never lost even if the mail server is down. 202 - Shops are checked side by side by a small worker pool, each at its own minute, with a 150-second watchdog per check. 203 204 **Watch this address:** signed-in users can also have any website (not just their shop) checked daily and get an email when something new goes wrong. Outside addresses are only ever *explained*, never changed. 205 206 --- 207 208 ## The shop itself 209 210 Every seller's site comes from **one rendering engine and one template**, server-rendered by FastAPI with Jinja2 and chosen by the `Host` header. There is no generated code and no per-seller CSS. 211 212 - **Six looks** for home businesses: Bakery & desserts, Home kitchen / tiffin, Handmade & crafts, Tailoring & custom work, Gifts & hampers, General. Claude picks only a **key** (which look, which accent, three short lines of copy). Code validates the key and draws everything: colours, self-hosted fonts, layout and illustrations. 213 - **Menu with prices in ₹**, a basket that works even without JavaScript, extras listed separately, a search box for long menus. 214 - **Order form** with date (minimum notice enforced), pickup or delivery (by area or PIN code), time slots, quantities, and totals worked out **on the server**. 215 - **Payment by UPI, only after an order**: the shop page never shows the seller's UPI ID or QR code. After a real order, the thank-you page (and the order's own private status page) shows "Pay ₹X via UPI" as a prefilled UPI link on phones and a QR code on laptops, with the exact amount and the order ID as the note. Pay-on-delivery orders get no UPI details at all. Money goes straight from the customer to the seller. It never passes through LaunchWitness. 216 - **"I've paid"**: after paying in their own UPI app, the customer can enter the 12-digit UPI reference (UTR) and, optionally, a screenshot (re-encoded, no hidden data). The seller sees **"Customer says paid"**, never "Paid": they check their own UPI app and mark the order Paid themselves. References and screenshots are private to the seller, and are deleted 30 days after the order closes. 217 - **Each shop's own signature**: a small set of drawings (sprinkles, leaves, stars and so on) chosen by code from the shop's name, shown as a strip under the top of the page where no text sits, plus gentle touches (add-to-basket, a quick view of each item). The page works the same with JavaScript off. 218 - **WhatsApp button**, an order status page per order, a privacy page, "Report this shop", and the optional food licence (FSSAI) number. 219 - **Product photos**: re-encoded to WebP from the pixels alone, so no location or camera data survives. 220 - **Accessibility and safety**: every colour combination passes WCAG AA (tested), every seller-supplied field is HTML-escaped (tested with hostile input in every field, in every look), and shop pages send a strict Content-Security-Policy. 221 222 Screenshots of every look: [`docs/screenshots/s14/contact-sheet.png`](docs/screenshots/s14/contact-sheet.png). 223 224 --- 225 226 ## Safety: why an AI can be trusted with this 227 228 The core rule: **the model decides and explains; plain code acts and checks.** 229 230 | Rule | How it's enforced | 231 |---|---| 232 | **Approve before spending** | A purchase in code needs **all three**: `ALLOW_PURCHASE=true` (off by default), a cost under the hard cap `MAX_SPEND_USD`, and a matching approval record from the owner. In practice, domains are bought by the owner on godaddy.com and then adopted. | 233 | **Preview before changing** | Every DNS change is shown as before → after on the approval card. | 234 | **Back up, then undo** | The current records are saved before any DNS write. A write without a backup is refused. A failed launch can be put back. | 235 | **Scoped writes** | A launch can only touch its own domain (or its own subdomain), one record type and name at a time. DNS is never written to a domain that isn't in the app's own database. | 236 | **Fixed repairs** | The Doctor can only choose from five fixes in code. Anything else is refused and logged. | 237 | **Everything audited** | Every change of state writes an `AuditEvent` (who, what, when, result), shown in the report. | 238 | **Sandbox by default** | `GODADDY_ENV=ote` (GoDaddy's test environment) unless production is set explicitly. | 239 | **No secrets in the repo** | All keys come from environment variables. `.env` exists only on the server. A secret scan of the repo and the whole git history is clean. | 240 | **Trust and safety for a public tool** | Sign-in by email link (no passwords); team approval before an account can launch for real; a Claude policy check that can only **hold** a shop for human review, never launch one (and holds if it fails); "Report this shop"; a team pause switch; rate limits per visitor and per account; a cap of 40 live shops. | 241 242 --- 243 244 ## How GoDaddy is used 245 246 GoDaddy is the engine, not decoration. 247 248 | Step | GoDaddy product | What LaunchWitness does with it | 249 |---|---|---| 250 | **Find a name** | Domains API | Availability and price for the names Claude suggests. | 251 | **Buy** | godaddy.com checkout | Done by the owner, then adopted after approval. The API purchase path exists but is locked behind the spend guards. | 252 | **Point and protect** | DNS API | Back up the zone; write scoped records (A, MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC); undo from backup. All calls share one rate limit (50 a minute, under GoDaddy's 60). | 253 | **Email** | GoDaddy Professional Email (Titan) | The app's mailbox sends every email over SMTP (`smtpout.secureserver.net`) and reads the inbox over IMAP to prove a test order arrived. | 254 | **Host** | GoDaddy Docker VPS | Runs everything. Caddy issues an HTTPS certificate for each shop on demand, but only for domains in the app's database. | 255 | **Verify** | GoDaddy's authoritative nameservers | Checks ask GoDaddy's own nameservers, not a cache, so the result is the real one. | 256 257 Hosting is the Docker VPS, not GoDaddy's Hosting API: one box runs the app and every seller site with automatic HTTPS. 258 259 --- 260 261 ## How Claude is used 262 263 Claude has three jobs, and none of them involve acting on money or DNS. 264 265 | Role | Model | Job | Output | 266 |---|---|---|---| 267 | **Reader** | Strong (`claude-sonnet-5-5`, vision) | Turn a messy description and price list (text or photo, English or Hinglish) into a strict profile, the shop's wording, and its look. Decide whether the business takes orders or bookings. | Profile JSON. Code tidies and validates every field. | 268 | **Namer** | Cheap (`claude-haiku-5-5`) | Suggest about ten names that fit the brand. | Names. Code checks availability and price. | 269 | **Doctor** | Cheap | Investigate a failed check with read-only tools and explain it in one sentence. | A finding plus a playbook fix id or "needs you". Code applies it. | 270 | **Policy check** | Cheap | Is this shop OK to put live? | OK, or "hold for review" with a reason. It can never launch or unpause. | 271 272 **Cost:** roughly 3 calls per launch plus 1 per failed check, a few cents in total. Every call has a tight `max_tokens`, and a daily spend cap stops live calls when reached. During development, saved responses ("fixtures") in `backend/tests/fixtures/` replace live calls, so the UI was built at $0 of API spend. Seller text and tool results are always passed as data, and a prompt-injection fixture is part of the test suite. 273 274 --- 275 276 ## Architecture 277 278 ``` 279 ┌──────────────── GoDaddy Docker VPS ─────────────────┐ 280 │ │ 281 browser / phone ───▶ │ Caddy │ 282 (app, shops, │ • HTTPS for the app and every shop │ 283 shared reports) │ • on-demand TLS, approved by an internal "ask" │ 284 │ endpoint (only domains in the database) │ 285 │ │ │ 286 │ ▼ │ 287 │ FastAPI app (one process) │──▶ GoDaddy Domains / DNS APIs 288 │ • JSON API + the built React app │──▶ Claude API 289 │ • seller shops (Jinja2, picked by Host header) │ (Reader, Namer, Doctor, policy) 290 │ • agents: Planner, Executor, Checker (code) │──▶ SMTP / IMAP (app mailbox) 291 │ • Doctor playbook (code) │──▶ public DNS + HTTPS probes 292 │ • outbox (every email saved, then retried) │ (through the SSRF guard) 293 │ • APScheduler monitoring + worker pool │ 294 │ • SQLite (WAL) on a volume, nightly backups │ 295 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ 296 ``` 297 298 ### The agents 299 300 | Agent | Claude or code | Job |

300 | Agent | Claude or code | Job | 301 |---|---|---| 302 | **Reader** | Claude | Description + price list → profile + copy + look | 303 | **Namer** | Claude suggests, code checks | Available names with real prices | 304 | **Policy** | Claude decides, code holds | OK to go live, or hold for a human | 305 | **Planner** | Code | Every step, every before → after setting, and the cost → the approval card | 306 | **Executor** | Code | Runs the approved plan with the guards, backup first, resumable step log | 307 | **Checker** | Code | Address, HTTPS, email settings, real test order, clean finish | 308 | **Doctor** | Claude chooses, code applies | Investigate, explain, pick a playbook fix, re-check | 309 310 ### Design decisions worth knowing 311 312 - **Every outside service sits behind one wrapper with a fake.** GoDaddy, Claude, SMTP, IMAP, DNS and HTTPS each have a real and an in-memory implementation (`app/integrations.py`). Practice mode (`USE_FAKES=true`) and the whole test suite run against the fakes, and tests block every real network call. 313 - **Practice and real launches run the same code.** Practice swaps the outside world for fakes; the shop page, order handler and checks are identical, and every practice row is labelled. 314 - **One A record per shop, no wildcard.** Each real shop gets exactly one DNS record written by the app, so a shop that doesn't exist doesn't resolve. 315 - **SQLite on purpose.** One VPS, one app process (the app refuses to start a second), WAL mode, online backups (7 daily + 4 weekly) with a tested restore. Moving to Postgres is a small change because every table is a SQLModel model. 316 - **The checker can't be turned into a weapon.** It reaches websites only through `SafeWeb`: it resolves the host once, refuses private, loopback and cloud-metadata addresses, pins the checked IP, and re-checks every redirect. 317 - **The app container uses public DNS resolvers.** The VPS's own resolvers returned wrong answers for some domains during testing, so the app asks 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1 and 9.9.9.9 instead. 318 319 --- 320 321 ## Tech stack 322 323 | Layer | Technology | 324 |---|---| 325 | Backend | Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLModel + SQLite, httpx, dnspython, APScheduler, Jinja2, Pillow, segno (QR codes), `anthropic` SDK | 326 | Frontend | React 18, Vite 5, TypeScript, plain CSS (no UI kit) | 327 | Seller sites | Server-rendered Jinja2, one template, six themes, self-hosted open-licence fonts | 328 | Infrastructure | GoDaddy Docker VPS, Docker Compose, Caddy (automatic HTTPS, on-demand TLS) | 329 | Email | GoDaddy Professional Email over SMTP and IMAP; Mailpit for the local stack | 330 | Testing | pytest (1,580+ backend tests), Playwright end-to-end flows, ruff | 331 332 --- 333 334 ## Repository layout 335 336 ``` 337 backend/ 338 app/ 339 main.py FastAPI app, routers, host-based shop routing 340 config.py settings from environment variables 341 models.py, db.py SQLite tables (Business, Plan, DnsBackup, Evidence, AuditEvent, Approval, ...) 342 agents/ reader, namer, policy, doctor, investigator (Claude); 343 planner, executor, checker, launch_check, playbook (code) 344 checks/ DNS lookups, HTTPS probes, email-settings checks, SSRF-safe fetch 345 godaddy/ GoDaddy API client (ote|prod, scoped DNS writes), availability, email, rate limit 346 sites/ shop rendering, themes, orders, fulfilment rules, templates, fonts 347 mail/ SMTP, IMAP, email layout 348 monitor/ scheduler for light monitoring 349 safety/ spend guard, access control, CSRF/origin guard, route table 350 proof.py, chain.py evidence rows and the hash chain 351 outbox.py every email saved first, then sent and retried 352 routers/ API routes (auth, businesses, launch, report, admin, watch, ...) 353 tests/ pytest suite + fixtures (saved Claude responses, sample sellers) 354 frontend/ React + Vite app (landing, describe, review, launch, report, orders, admin) 355 e2e/ Playwright end-to-end tests 356 deploy/ Dockerfile, docker-compose files, Caddyfile (local) and Caddyfile.prod 357 scripts/ backups, checks, demo seeding, screenshots, secret scan, replay builder 358 docs/ spec, build plan, progress, build log, security, checks matrix, runbooks, screenshots 359 replay/ redacted Claude Code session transcripts (served at /build) 360 ``` 361 362 --- 363 364 ## Running it yourself 365 366 ### Option 1: practice mode on your machine (no keys needed) 367 368 Practice mode uses in-memory fakes for GoDaddy, DNS, the mailbox and HTTPS, and saved Claude responses, so you don't need any API keys. 369 370 ```bash 371 cp .env.example .env # defaults are safe: fakes on, sandbox, purchases off 372 python3.12 -m venv .venv 373 .venv/bin/pip install -r backend/requirements-dev.txt 374 (cd frontend && npm install && npm run build) 375 376 cd backend 377 ../.venv/bin/pytest -q # run the tests (no network) 378 ../.venv/bin/uvicorn app.main:app --port 8000 379 ``` 380 381 Open http://localhost:8000. For local development set `DEV_MODE=true` in `.env` so sign-in links appear on screen instead of being emailed (it refuses to start on https). `cd frontend && npm run dev` runs the frontend with hot reload and proxies `/api` to port 8000. 382 383 > **On Windows**, use `.venv/Scripts/python -m pytest` and `.venv/Scripts/python -m uvicorn ...` instead. 384 385 ### Option 2: the full stack with Docker 386 387 ```bash 388 docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml up --build # → http://localhost 389 ``` 390 391 A production-like stack (real HTTPS through Caddy's local certificate authority, `DEV_MODE=false`, fakes, and Mailpit to catch emails at http://localhost:8025): 392 393 ```bash 394 docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml \ 395 -f deploy/docker-compose.local.yml up -d --build --wait # → https://launchwitness.localhost 396 bash scripts/check_m1.sh --local # automated checks of the running stack 397 ``` 398 399 ### Option 3: production on a VPS 400 401 Follow [`docs/RUNBOOK_M1.md`](docs/RUNBOOK_M1.md) and [`docs/NEXT_SESSION_VPS.md`](docs/NEXT_SESSION_VPS.md). In short: fill `.env` on the server (never in the repo), then 402 403 ```bash 404 docker compose --env-file .env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml up -d --build 405 bash scripts/check_m1.sh 406 ``` 407 408 Backups: `bash scripts/backup_db.sh` (7 daily + 4 weekly), restore with `bash scripts/restore_db.sh `. 409 410 ### Rehearsing the demo 411 412 ```bash 413 python3 scripts/seed_demo.py --launched # creates Meera's shop and runs a practice launch 414 python3 scripts/seed_demo.py --reset # removes it 415 ``` 416 417 To show the Doctor at work, sign in as the team (`ADMIN_EMAIL`), open a shop's report, and use the demo switch to stage a fault: the address leads nowhere, a parked page, a broken padlock, or a refused mail sign-in. The fault is staged so the demo is reliable; detecting and fixing it is real code. 418 419 ### Key environment variables 420 421 All are listed in [`.env.example`](.env.example) with safe defaults. 422 423 | Variable | Default | Meaning | 424 |---|---|---| 425 | `USE_FAKES` | `true` | Use in-memory fakes for every outside service | 426 | `GODADDY_ENV` | `ote` | GoDaddy sandbox; `prod` only when set explicitly | 427 | `ALLOW_PURCHASE` | `false` | Purchases are impossible unless turned on | 428 | `MAX_SPEND_USD` | `15` | Hard limit on any single purchase | 429 | `CLAUDE_MODE` | `fixture` | `fixture` uses saved responses; `live` calls the API | 430 | `CLAUDE_DAILY_SPEND_CAP_USD` | `3` | Live Claude calls stop when reached | 431 | `DNS_MODE` | `per_shop` | One A record per shop (or `wildcard`) | 432 | `MONITOR_ENABLED` | `true` | Background monitoring (tests never start it) | 433 | `MAX_LIVE_SHOPS` | `40` | Upper limit on real shops | 434 435 --- 436 437 ## Testing 438 439 ```bash 440 cd backend && ../.venv/bin/pytest -q # 1,580+ tests, no network access allowed 441 .venv/bin/python -m ruff check backend # lint 442 cd frontend && npx tsc --noEmit && npm run build 443 cd e2e && npm install && npx playwright install chromium && npx playwright test 444 bash scripts/secret_scan.sh # secrets in the repo and the whole git history 445 ``` 446 447 What the tests cover, among other things: 448 449 - **Every check scenario** in [`docs/CHECKS_MATRIX.md`](docs/CHECKS_MATRIX.md): about forty website and email situations, each with the exact wording shown, how sure it is, and what the Doctor may do. 450 - **Access control:** every owner route tested as owner, another seller, a guest, logged out and admin. A test fails if any route is missing from the route table. 451 - **XSS:** a hostile string in every free-text field, every product field and the order form, parsed with a real HTML parser, in every theme. 452 - **SSRF:** private ranges, redirect re-checks, IP pinning, redirect loops. 453 - **Safety guards:** purchases blocked without all three conditions, DNS writes refused without a backup or outside the database. 454 - **The Claude agents** against saved real responses, including a prompt-injection seller and a handwritten price-list photo. 455 - **End-to-end flows** in a real browser: a full seller journey, two sellers who must not see each other's shops, guest practice, sign-in, legal pages, every theme launched in practice with no console errors or CSP violations, and more. 456 457 --- 458 459 ## Security 460 461 A one-page overview is in [`docs/SECURITY.md`](docs/SECURITY.md). Highlights: 462 463 - **Ownership checks** are part of the database query, so another owner's shop answers 404, the same as one that doesn't exist. 464 - **CSRF:** every state-changing request needs the app's Origin and a token bound to the session cookie. 465 - **Cookies** are `__Host-` prefixed, Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax with no Domain, so shop subdomains never receive them. 466 - **Tokens** (sign-in, share, "Yes, I got it") are 32 random bytes and only their SHA-256 hash is stored. 467 - **Uploads** are size-capped, checked by content, and the price-list photo is never stored. 468 - **The certificate "ask" endpoint** is closed to the public at both Caddy and the app. 469 - **Privacy:** a customer's street address appears only on the owner's Orders page and in the order email, never in logs, evidence or the shared report. 470 471 --- 472 473 ## What's real today, and what isn't yet 474 475 Being honest about the state of a hackathon build: 476 477 **Real and running in production** 478 479 - The app at https://launchwitness.com on a GoDaddy Docker VPS, with Let's Encrypt HTTPS. 480 - A real shop launched by the app: its DNS record written through the GoDaddy API with a backup first, its certificate issued on demand, all seven checks proven, and a shareable report with an intact evidence chain. 481 - Real email: sign-in links, order emails and test orders sent through GoDaddy Professional Email, and test orders found in the inbox over IMAP. 482 - Monitoring, nightly database backups, and a tested restore. 483 - Private UPI: the live shops show UPI details only after an order, and customers can tell the shop they paid (UTR and an optional screenshot), which the seller checks before marking the order Paid. 484 485 **Not done yet** 486 487 - **Real launches on the seller's own domain** were cut for this round. They work in practice mode; real launches use a free `.launchwitness.com` address. 488 - **Creating a mailbox for each seller** through GoDaddy's email API is still a stub. Test orders go to the app's own mailbox, or the owner confirms with "Yes, I got it". 489 - **The admin** is whoever controls the `ADMIN_EMAIL` inbox. There is no second factor yet. 490 - **The demo fault** is staged so it shows reliably on camera. The detection and the fix are real. 491 - **Payments** are UPI links only. No money passes through LaunchWitness, so it never confirms a payment: "Customer says paid" stays a claim until the seller checks their UPI app. Card payments (a gateway, after the seller's KYC) are future work. 492 493 --- 494 495 ## How it was built 496 497 The whole product was built in **Claude Code**, over recorded sessions, each following a fixed ritual written in [`CLAUDE.md`](CLAUDE.md): 498 499 1. Read the progress file and propose a plan mapped to the acceptance criteria in [`docs/BUILD_PLAN.md`](docs/BUILD_PLAN.md). 500 2. Wait for the owner's OK before coding. 501 3. Make small, tested commits. 502 4. Update [`docs/PROGRESS.md`](docs/PROGRESS.md) and [`docs/BUILD_LOG.md`](docs/BUILD_LOG.md), then save a transcript that is redacted and secret-scanned before it is committed. 503 504 Product decisions (scope, safety rules, budget, what to postpone) stayed with the human. When the spec didn't answer something, the simplest option was chosen and recorded under "Decisions". A few hard rules held across every session: no secrets in the repo, Claude Code never spends money, GoDaddy defaults to the sandbox, and live Claude calls during development were kept to a minimum by using saved responses. 505 506 Every feature session ended with a check in a real browser at phone width, which caught real bugs. The full record is replayed at **https://launchwitness.com/build**, and a human-written summary of each session is in [`docs/BUILD_LOG.md`](docs/BUILD_LOG.md). 507 508 --- 509 510 ## What's next 511 512 1. **Run on the seller's own GoDaddy account**, so they own everything and monitoring matters most. 513 2. **Own-domain launches and per-seller mailboxes**, using the guarded purchase path and GoDaddy's email API. 514 3. **Change detection:** when a setting changes, ask "Was this you? Tap to restore" instead of fixing silently. 515 4. **A `/verify` page** backed by a DNS TXT record, so buyers can tell a seller's real shop from a fake using their name. 516 5. **More trades and languages:** bookings for salons and tutors, more Indian languages for the description. 517 6. **Card payments** ("Connect Razorpay") after the seller's KYC. 518 519 --- 520 521 ## Further reading 522 523 | Document | What's in it | 524 |---|---| 525 | [`docs/SPEC.md`](docs/SPEC.md) | The full product spec | 526 | [`docs/BUILD_PLAN.md`](docs/BUILD_PLAN.md) | Milestones and acceptance criteria | 527 | [`docs/CHECKS_MATRIX.md`](docs/CHECKS_MATRIX.md) | Every check scenario, its wording, and the test that proves it | 528 | [`docs/SECURITY.md`](docs/SECURITY.md) | Security on one page | 529 | [`docs/PROGRESS.md`](docs/PROGRESS.md) | Status, decisions and open questions | 530 | [`docs/BUILD_LOG.md`](docs/BUILD_LOG.md) | One entry per build session | 531 | [`docs/RUNBOOK_M1.md`](docs/RUNBOOK_M1.md) | Going live on the VPS, step by step | 532 | [`deploy/README.md`](deploy/README.md) | The Docker setup in detail | 533 | [`e2e/README.md`](e2e/README.md) | Running the end-to-end tests | 534 535 --- 536 537

LaunchWitness

From business idea to customer-ready.
Be ready before your first customer arrives.

Submission for the GoDaddy Inclusive Innovation Hackathon 2026 (Round 2, Open Innovation)

LaunchWitness builds a home seller's online shop, puts it online on GoDaddy, **places a real test order through the shop's own order form and proves it reaches the seller's inbox**, fixes what breaks from a fixed list of safe repairs, and keeps checking after launch. ## Live links | What | Link | |---|---| | The app | https://launchwitness.com | | A real shop launched by the app (Meera's demo bakery) | https://meeras-eggless-bakes.launchwitness.com | | A demo shop (sample, orders are not real) | https://launchwitness.com/demo/meera | | That shop's shared proof report | https://launchwitness.com/r/GsZj7gOAoCydSauqdNpoaWksKHVW-HSz | | Recompute the report's evidence chain yourself | https://launchwitness.com/r/GsZj7gOAoCydSauqdNpoaWksKHVW-HSz/verify | | How it was built with Claude Code (session replay) | https://launchwitness.com/build | **Trying it as a judge, no account needed:** open https://launchwitness.com, press **Try it without an account**, pick an example seller, review the shop, and run a **practice launch**. Practice mode runs every step against a pretend GoDaddy: nothing is bought and nothing goes on the internet. Then open the eight demo shops from the strip on the landing page (`/demo/meera`, `/demo/imran`, `/demo/sunita`, ...). --- ## The problem Many home sellers in India (cakes, tiffins, tailoring, crafts, gift hampers) take orders in Instagram and WhatsApp messages. When they do get a website, nobody checks that it actually works end to end. A missing email setting sends order emails to spam; a form posts to nowhere; an address stops pointing at the shop. The seller sees no error message. She just gets fewer orders and thinks business is slow. Our demo persona is **Meera**, who bakes eggless cakes at home in Pune. She doesn't know what DNS is, and she shouldn't have to. What she needs to know is one thing: **if a customer orders, will I get it?** --- ## How it works, in five steps | # | Step | Who does it | What happens | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | **Describe** | Seller + Claude | She types a few lines and pastes her price list (or uploads a photo of it, even handwritten). Claude reads it into a structured shop: items and prices in ₹, sizes, notice needed, pickup or delivery, hours, area. | | 2 | **Review** | Seller | The shop appears as an ordinary form and a private preview. She fixes anything wrong, adds photos, picks one of six looks, and marks items that take custom requests. No AI involved. | | 3 | **Launch on GoDaddy** | Code only, after she approves | One approval card shows every step, every setting as before → after, and the cost. On approval, code backs up the DNS records, writes the shop's record through the GoDaddy API, and the server issues HTTPS for the shop. | | 4 | **Prove a real order reaches her** | Code | The checker opens her public shop page, fills in the real order form like a customer, and follows that order: form accepted → mail server accepted → **found in the inbox** (read over IMAP) or **confirmed by her** ("Yes, I got it" link in the test email). It also checks the address, HTTPS and the email settings. The report says "ready for customers" only when every check passed. | | 5 | **Fix and keep watching** | Claude explains, code fixes | A failed check is explained in one plain sentence and repaired from a playbook of five fixes in code, then checked again. After launch the shop is re-checked every 15 minutes (site, HTTPS) and daily (settings, expiry dates, a test order to LaunchWitness's own check mailbox). Problems are emailed to her personal address. | After launch she also gets an **Orders** page (New → Confirmed → Paid → Done / Cancelled) and an email for every order. --- ## What Claude does, and what plain code does The rule: **Claude decides and explains; plain code acts and checks.** Claude never spends money and never writes DNS. | Claude (judgment) | Model | Job | |---|---|---| | **Reader** | Strong (`claude-sonnet-5-5`) | Turns her messy description and price list (text or photo, English or Hinglish) into a strict shop profile, its wording and its look. Code validates and tidies every field. | | **Namer** | Cheap (`claude-haiku-5-5`) | Suggests about ten shop names. Code checks which are available and what they cost. | | **Doctor / Investigator** | Cheap | Looks at a failed check with read-only tools (look up the shop's own address, fetch its own page, read stored evidence, test the mail server sign-in without sending), then explains it in one sentence and picks a fix id from the playbook, or says "needs you". | | **Policy check** | Cheap | Is this shop OK to put live? It can only **hold** a shop for a human to look at. It can never launch or unpause one. | | Plain code (guarded, audited) | Job | |---|---| | **Money** | A purchase needs all three: `ALLOW_PURCHASE=true` (off by default), a cost under `MAX_SPEND_USD`, and the owner's approval record. In this build the app never bought anything. | | **DNS** | Planner shows every change as before → after; Executor backs up first, writes only to domains in the app's own database, one record at a time, and can undo from the backup. | | **Rendering** | One template draws every shop, server-side. Claude only picks keys (which look, which accent); code draws everything. | | **Checks** | The Checker proves each claim and stores it as evidence. The Doctor's chosen fix is applied by code, and only if it is in the playbook and allowed for that check. | Every state change writes an audit row (who, what, when, result). If Claude is unavailable or over its daily budget, plain rules take over: the launch check holds, and the Doctor falls back to a standard fix or clear instructions. --- ## How GoDaddy is load-bearing | GoDaddy product | What LaunchWitness does with it | |---|---| | **Domain** | `launchwitness.com` is registered at GoDaddy. Every real shop lives at `.launchwitness.com`. | | **DNS API** | At launch the app backs up the zone's records, then writes one A record for the shop through the GoDaddy API (guarded client, scoped to its own records). The demo shop's record was written this way. Undo restores from the backup. | | **Authoritative nameservers** | The address check asks GoDaddy's own nameservers, not a cache, so the answer is the real one. | | **VPS (Docker)** | One GoDaddy VPS runs everything with Docker Compose: Caddy (HTTPS for the app and an on-demand certificate for each shop, only for shops in the database) and the FastAPI app. | | **Professional Email (Titan) mailbox** | `hello@launchwitness.com`. The app sends every email (sign-in links, order emails, test orders, the contact form) over **SMTP** (`smtpout.secureserver.net`), and reads the inbox over **IMAP** to prove a test order arrived. | | **HTTPS** | Let's Encrypt certificates through Caddy, for the apex, `www` and each shop subdomain. | --- ## Hackathon requirements: how to verify each one | Requirement | Where | How to check it | |---|---|---| | Live app hosted on GoDaddy | GoDaddy VPS | Open https://launchwitness.com | | Own domain over HTTPS | `launchwitness.com` (GoDaddy) | The padlock on https://launchwitness.com and https://meeras-eggless-bakes.launchwitness.com | | A mailbox that receives a test email | `hello@launchwitness.com` (GoDaddy Professional Email) | The shared report's test-order row: "found in the inbox" with the time, read over IMAP | | Contact form delivers to the mailbox via SMTP | Landing page, "Contact us" | `backend/app/routers/contact.py` sends to `SMTP_USER` through the SMTP mailer; each message is audited | | No password in code or repo | `.env` exists only on the server | `bash scripts/secret_scan.sh` scans the repo and the whole git history; `.env.example` has no values | --- ## Safety - **Strict Content-Security-Policy on every shop page.** Scripts run only if their hash matches the template's own fixed scripts, so a script that came from a seller's words could never run. - **Escaping, tested.** Every seller-supplied and customer-supplied field is HTML-escaped. Tests put a hostile string into every field, in every one of the six looks, and in the order email. - **Private UPI.** A shop page never shows the seller's UPI ID or QR code. Only after a real order does the thank-you page (and the order's own private status page) show a UPI link and QR for the exact amount. A customer can then say "I've paid" with the 12-digit UPI reference and an optional screenshot. The seller sees **"Customer says paid"**, never "Paid": she checks her own UPI app first. - **Held edits.** When a live shop's owner changes its words, the policy check runs again; if it isn't sure, the edit waits for the team and the shop stays live as it was. - **Spend caps.** Purchases are off by default and capped; Claude has a daily spend cap; every Claude call has a tight `max_tokens`. - **Tamper-evident evidence.** Every claim on a report comes from a stored evidence row. Each shop's rows form an append-only hash chain. Anyone with the report link can open `/verify` and the server recomputes the chain: "Intact", or exactly which row changed. - **Uploads.** Product photos, payment screenshots and custom-order reference photos all go through one gate: size cap, content sniff (JPEG, PNG or WebP by what the file is, not its name), pixel cap, then a brand-new image is drawn from the pixels alone, so no location or camera data survives. Screenshots and reference photos are owner-only and deleted 30 days after the order is done or cancelled. - **The checker can't be pointed at private addresses.** It reaches websites only through an SSRF guard (private, loopback and cloud-metadata addresses refused, IP pinned, every redirect re-checked). More in [`docs/SECURITY.md`](docs/SECURITY.md). --- ## Custom orders Photo cakes, theme cakes, tailoring and custom gifts need the seller to **see** what the customer wants before she accepts. An item can be marked **"Takes custom requests"** (the Reader sets it only from the seller's own words, such as "photo cake" or "stitching"; she can switch it on Review). When a customer's basket has such an item, the order form asks "Tell us what you want" for that item (up to 500 characters) and allows **one** reference photo (JPG, PNG or WebP, up to 5 MB). The seller sees both on her Orders page. The order email carries the notes and says "Reference photo: open it in Orders"; the photo is never attached and never has a public link. --- ## What's real today, and what is practice mode **Real, running in production on the GoDaddy VPS** - The app at https://launchwitness.com with Let's Encrypt HTTPS. - One real shop launched by the app: Meera's demo bakery. Its DNS record was written through the GoDaddy API with a backup first, its certificate was issued on demand, and its shared report shows every check proven with an intact evidence chain. - Real email through GoDaddy Professional Email: sign-in links, order emails, test orders (found in the inbox over IMAP) and the contact form. - Monitoring, nightly database backups with a tested restore. - Live Claude calls for the Reader, Namer, Doctor and policy check, under a daily spend cap. **Practice mode (clearly labelled "Practice" everywhere)** - Guests and new accounts launch in practice mode: the same code runs against in-memory fakes of GoDaddy, DNS, the mailbox and HTTPS. Nothing is bought and nothing goes on the internet. - The eight `/demo/*` shops are samples: their order form places no order and stores nothing, and their WhatsApp button opens a page that says it is a demo. **Not done yet** - **Launches on a seller's own domain** were cut for this round. They work in practice mode; real launches use a free `.launchwitness.com` address. No domain was bought by the app. - **Creating a mailbox per seller** through GoDaddy's email API is still a stub. Order emails go to the seller's verified sign-in email. - **Payments** are UPI links only. No money passes through LaunchWitness, so it never confirms a payment. - **The demo fault switch** (for showing the Doctor on camera) stages a fault; detecting and repairing it is real code. - **The admin** is whoever controls the admin email inbox; there is no second factor yet. --- ## Tech stack | Layer | Technology | |---|---| | Backend | Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLModel + SQLite (WAL), httpx, dnspython, APScheduler, Jinja2, Pillow, `anthropic` SDK | | Frontend | React + Vite + TypeScript, plain CSS | | Seller shops | Server-rendered Jinja2, one template, six looks, self-hosted open-licence fonts | | Infrastructure | GoDaddy VPS, Docker Compose, Caddy (automatic HTTPS, on-demand TLS) | | Email | GoDaddy Professional Email over SMTP and IMAP; Mailpit for the local stack | | Tests | pytest, Playwright, ruff | --- ## Run it locally Practice mode needs no keys: fakes for every outside service and saved Claude responses. ```bash cp .env.example .env # safe defaults: fakes on, sandbox, purchases off python3.12 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/pip install -r backend/requirements-dev.txt (cd frontend && npm install && npm run build) cd backend && ../.venv/bin/uvicorn app.main:app --port 8000 # http://localhost:8000 ``` Set `DEV_MODE=true` in `.env` so sign-in links show on screen instead of being emailed. On Windows use `.venv/Scripts/python -m uvicorn ...`. A production-like stack (HTTPS through Caddy's local CA, fakes, Mailpit at http://localhost:8025): ```bash docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml \ -f deploy/docker-compose.local.yml up -d --build --wait # https://launchwitness.localhost bash scripts/check_m1.sh --local ``` Production on the VPS: [`docs/RUNBOOK_M1.md`](docs/RUNBOOK_M1.md) and [`docs/NEXT_SESSION_VPS.md`](docs/NEXT_SESSION_VPS.md). --- ## Tests ```bash cd backend && ../.venv/bin/pytest -q # tests block every real network call .venv/bin/python -m ruff check backend cd frontend && npx tsc --noEmit && npm run build cd e2e && npm install && npx playwright install chromium && npx playwright test # against the Docker stack bash scripts/secret_scan.sh ``` Results from the final session's runs (20 Nov 2026): TEST_COUNTS_PLACEHOLDER What they cover, among other things: every check scenario in [`docs/CHECKS_MATRIX.md`](docs/CHECKS_MATRIX.md); access control for every route (a test fails if a route is missing from the route table); hostile input in every field in every look; SSRF; the spend and DNS guards; the Claude agents against saved real responses, including a prompt-injection seller and a handwritten price-list photo; and browser flows from describing a shop to a customer's order arriving on the Orders page. --- ## Screenshots | | | |---|---| | Landing page (1440 px) ![Landing](docs/screenshots/s22/hero-1440.png) | Meera's live shop on a phone ![Live shop](docs/screenshots/s20b/live-demo-shop-390.png) | | The proof report ![Report](docs/screenshots/s12/10-report-1440.png) | The seller's Orders page ![Orders](docs/screenshots/s10-5/07-orders-page-1440.png) | All six shop looks: [`docs/screenshots/s14/contact-sheet.png`](docs/screenshots/s14/contact-sheet.png). --- ## Built with Claude Code The whole product was built in Claude Code, in recorded sessions that followed one written ritual ([`CLAUDE.md`](CLAUDE.md)): read the progress file, propose a plan against the acceptance criteria in [`docs/BUILD_PLAN.md`](docs/BUILD_PLAN.md), make small tested commits, update [`docs/PROGRESS.md`](docs/PROGRESS.md) and [`docs/BUILD_LOG.md`](docs/BUILD_LOG.md), and save a redacted, secret-scanned transcript. Product decisions stayed with the human. Hard rules held in every session: no secrets in the repo, Claude Code never spends money, GoDaddy defaults to the sandbox, and live Claude calls during development were kept to a minimum by using saved responses. The sessions are replayed at **https://launchwitness.com/build**. --- ## Further reading | Document | What's in it | |---|---| | [`docs/PROJECT_BRIEF.md`](docs/PROJECT_BRIEF.md) | The one-to-two page brief | | [`docs/JUDGE_QA.md`](docs/JUDGE_QA.md) | Short answers to likely questions | | [`docs/SPEC.md`](docs/SPEC.md) | The full product spec | | [`docs/CHECKS_MATRIX.md`](docs/CHECKS_MATRIX.md) | Every check scenario, its wording and its test | | [`docs/SECURITY.md`](docs/SECURITY.md) | Security on one page | | [`docs/BUILD_LOG.md`](docs/BUILD_LOG.md) | One entry per build session | | [`deploy/README.md`](deploy/README.md) · [`e2e/README.md`](e2e/README.md) | Docker setup · end-to-end tests |

Built for the GoDaddy Inclusive Innovation Hackathon 2026. LaunchWitness is a working name.

-Most tools would call a site "live" once the page loads. LaunchWitness is stricter. Each claim on the report comes from a stored `Evidence` row, and each hop is recorded separately:
+The rule: **Claude decides and explains; plain code acts and checks.** Claude never spends money and never writes DNS.
-| Check | How it's proven | Why it's done this way |

-| **The address leads to the shop** | Asked of the domain's **own authoritative nameservers** (found from its NS records), not a cached resolver. The answering server is recorded. -## Safety: why an AI can be trusted with this
-The core rule: **the model decides and explains; plain code acts and checks.**
+- **Strict Content-Security-Policy on every shop page.** Scripts run only if their hash matches the template's own fixed scripts, so a script that came from a seller's words could never run.
+- **Escaping, tested.** Every seller-supplied and customer-supplied field is HTML-escaped. Tests put a hostile string into every field, in every one of the six looks, and in the order email.

+- **Private UPI.** A shop page never shows the seller's UPI ID or QR code. Only after a real order does the thank-you page (and the order's own private status page) show a UPI link and QR for the exact amount. A customer can then say "I've paid" with the 12-digit UPI reference and an optional screenshot. The seller sees **"Customer says paid"**, never "Paid": she checks her own UPI app first.
+- **Held edits.** When a live shop's owner changes its words, the policy check runs again; if it isn't sure, the edit waits for the team and the shop stays live as it was.
+- **Spend caps.** Purchases are off by default and capped; Claude has a daily spend cap; every Claude call has a tight `max_tokens`.

+- **Tamper-evident evidence.** Every claim on a report comes from a stored evidence row. Each shop's rows form an append-only hash chain. Anyone with the report link can open `/verify` and the server recomputes the chain: "Intact", or exactly which row changed.

+- **Uploads.** Product photos, payment screenshots and custom-order reference photos all go through one gate: size cap, content sniff (JPEG, PNG or WebP by what the file is, not its name), pixel cap, then a brand-new image is drawn from the pixels alone, so no location or camera data survives. Screenshots and reference photos are owner-only and deleted 30 days after the order is done or cancelled.

+- **The checker can't be pointed at private addresses.** It reaches websites only through an SSRF guard (private, loopback and cloud-metadata addresses refused, IP pinned, every redirect re-checked).

# LaunchWitness: short answers for judges

**Isn't this just a website builder, or GoDaddy Airo?**
No. Building the shop is step one of five, and the least new one. What LaunchWitness adds is the part no builder
does: after the shop goes live, it places a real test order through the shop's own public order form and follows it
until it is found in the inbox (or the seller taps "Yes, I got it"). It checks the address, HTTPS and email settings,
repairs what fails from a fixed playbook, and keeps checking after launch. The report only says "ready for customers"
when every check has passed, and each claim is backed by stored, tamper-evident evidence.

**How does the seller know a customer paid?**
She checks her own UPI app. After a real order the customer sees a UPI link and QR code for the exact amount, with
the order reference as the payment note. After paying, the customer can enter the 12-digit UPI reference (and an
optional screenshot). The seller's Orders page then shows **"Customer says paid"**, never "Paid". She marks the order
Paid herself once she sees the money. LaunchWitness never sees a bank and never claims a payment happened.

**Why no payment gateway?**
A gateway needs the seller's KYC, a business bank account and fees, which is a real barrier for a home seller who
already gets paid by UPI every day. UPI links move money straight from the customer to the seller; nothing passes
through LaunchWitness. Card payments through a gateway are listed as future work.

**Why hide the UPI ID on the shop page?**
A UPI ID on a public page can be copied onto a fake shop, and it invites payments with no order behind them. So the
shop page says how payment works but shows no ID or QR. The UPI details appear only after a real order, on the
thank-you page and the order's own unguessable status page, with the exact amount and the order reference.

**What if Claude is wrong, or someone hides instructions in their shop description?**
Claude never acts. It returns data (a profile, names, a finding, a fix id, OK or hold), and code validates every
field. The Doctor can only pick from five fixes written in code; anything else is refused and logged. The seller's
text and every tool result are passed to Claude as data, and a prompt-injection seller is part of the test suite.
The Reader's output is shown to the seller on Review before anything goes live. The policy check can only hold a shop
for a human; it can never launch one.

**What if the Claude API is down or over budget?**
Every call has a tight `max_tokens` and there is a daily spend cap. When Claude can't answer: the policy check fails
closed (the shop is held for the team, not launched), the Doctor falls back to plain rules (a single allowed standard
fix, or clear instructions for the owner), and the Reader shows a plain message asking the seller to try again.
Checks, repairs and monitoring are plain code and keep working.

**What does it cost to run?**
One GoDaddy VPS, the `launchwitness.com` domain and one GoDaddy Professional Email mailbox, all from hackathon credit;
real shops use free subdomains, so no domain is bought per seller. Claude is a few calls per launch: the Reader
(strong model) once, the Namer and the policy check (cheap model) once each, and the Doctor only when a check fails.
The live Claude spend is capped per day in configuration.

**How do custom orders work?**
An item can be marked "Takes custom requests" (photo cakes, theme cakes, tailoring, custom gifts). The Reader sets
it only when the seller's own words say so, and she can switch it on Review. When a customer orders such an item, the
form asks "Tell us what you want" for it (up to 500 characters: the message on the cake, the design, measurements)
and allows one reference photo (JPG, PNG or WebP, up to 5 MB). The photo is re-drawn from its pixels (no location or
camera data), is visible only to the seller on her Orders page, is never attached to an email or given a public
link, and is deleted 30 days after the order is done or cancelled.

**Isn't it one template?**
Yes, on purpose: one rendering engine and one template, server-rendered. That is what makes every shop testable and
safe (strict CSP, escaping tested in every look, the checker's marker on every page). Within it there are six looks
for home businesses (bakery, home kitchen, handmade, tailoring, gifts, general), each with accent colours, its own
fonts and a per-shop drawn signature, plus the seller's own photos. Claude picks keys; code draws everything.

# LaunchWitness: from business idea to customer-ready

*GoDaddy Inclusive Innovation Hackathon 2026 · Round 2 · Open Innovation*

> **A real order reaches you, proven.** LaunchWitness puts a home seller's shop online on GoDaddy, places a real test
> order through the shop's own form, and shows her it arrived in her inbox before her first customer does. It fixes
> what breaks and keeps checking.

Live: https://launchwitness.com · A real launched shop: https://meeras-eggless-bakes.launchwitness.com ·
Its proof report: https://launchwitness.com/r/GsZj7gOAoCydSauqdNpoaWksKHVW-HSz · Build replay: https://launchwitness.com/build

## The problem

Home sellers in India (cakes, tiffins, tailoring, crafts, gift hampers) take orders in Instagram and WhatsApp
messages. A website could bring them customers, but setting one up is technical, and nobody checks it end to end.
A missing email setting sends orders to spam; an address stops pointing at the shop. There is no error message. The
seller just gets fewer orders. Her first sale becomes her first problem.

## The user

**Meera** bakes eggless cakes at home in Pune. She has a phone, a price list and customers who message her. She does
not know what DNS is. She needs one answer: if a customer orders, will I get it?

## The solution

1. **Describe.** She types a few lines and pastes her price list, or photographs it. Claude reads it into a shop.
2. **Review.** She checks it as an ordinary form with a private preview, adds photos, picks one of six looks.
3. **Launch on GoDaddy.** One approval card shows every change and the cost. Code backs up DNS, writes the shop's
   record through the GoDaddy API, and HTTPS is issued for the shop.
4. **Prove.** The checker places a real test order through her public order form and follows it: form accepted →
   mail server accepted → found in the inbox over IMAP (or she taps "Yes, I got it"). It also checks the address
   (asking GoDaddy's own nameservers), HTTPS and the email settings. Only when every check passes does the report say
   "ready for customers". Every claim is stored as evidence in a tamper-evident hash chain that anyone with the link
   can re-verify.
5. **Fix and keep watching.** A failed check is explained in one plain sentence and repaired from five fixes written
   in code, then checked again. After launch: the site every 15 minutes, settings and expiry dates daily.

Around the proof, the shop does what her customers need: a menu in ₹ with sizes, pickup or delivery, a date picker
that knows her notice and days off, UPI payment shown only after an order (with "Customer says paid" for her to check),
custom requests with a reference photo for photo cakes and tailoring, and an Orders page.

## Demo flow (about three minutes)

1. Landing page → **Try it without an account** → pick Meera → her shop appears on Review.
2. Run a practice launch: watch each step and each check; open the report.
3. Open the real launched shop and its shared report; press **Verify** to recompute the evidence chain.
4. Place an order on the shop; it appears on the Orders page and in the email.
5. Use the demo fault switch: a check fails, the Doctor explains it in one sentence, applies a playbook fix, and the
   check turns green again.

## How Claude is used

Claude **decides and explains**; plain code **acts and checks**. The Reader (strong model) turns her words into a
validated shop profile. The Namer suggests names; code checks availability and price. The Doctor investigates a
failed check with read-only tools and picks a fix id from a fixed playbook, or says "needs you". The policy check can
only hold a shop for a human. Claude never spends money and never writes DNS. Calls are capped by `max_tokens` and a
daily budget; if Claude is unavailable, plain rules take over and the policy check fails closed.

## How GoDaddy is used

GoDaddy is load-bearing. The domain `launchwitness.com`; the **DNS API** for each shop's record, always backed up
first and limited to the app's own domains; **GoDaddy's authoritative nameservers** as the source of truth for the
address check; one **GoDaddy VPS** running Docker (Caddy for HTTPS, the FastAPI app); and a **GoDaddy Professional
Email** mailbox that sends every email over SMTP and is read over IMAP to prove the test order arrived.

## Impact

A home seller gets a shop she can share with confidence, because she has seen proof that an order reaches her, and
she hears about a problem before her customers do. She keeps taking payments by UPI as she does today, and she never
has to learn what an MX record is. Practice mode lets anyone try the full flow without an account or any spending.

## What's next

- Launches on the seller's own domain and a mailbox per seller, through the guarded purchase path and GoDaddy's email API.
- Running on the seller's own GoDaddy account, so she owns everything.
- "Was this you?" when a setting changes, instead of a silent fix.
- Bookings for salons and tutors, and more Indian languages for the description.
- Card payments through a gateway once a seller has done KYC.

# LaunchWitness: short answers for judges

**Isn't this just a website builder, or GoDaddy Airo?**
No. Building the shop is step one of five, and the least new one. What LaunchWitness adds is the part no builder
does: after the shop goes live, it places a real test order through the shop's own public order form and follows it
until it is found in the inbox (or the seller taps "Yes, I got it"). It checks the address, HTTPS and email settings,
repairs what fails from a fixed playbook, and keeps checking after launch. The report only says "ready for customers"
when every check has passed, and each claim is backed by stored, tamper-evident evidence.

**How does the seller know a customer paid?**
She checks her own UPI app. After a real order the customer sees a UPI link and QR code for the exact amount, with
the order reference as the payment note. After paying, the customer can enter the 12-digit UPI reference (and an
optional screenshot). The seller's Orders page then shows **"Customer says paid"**, never "Paid". She marks the order
Paid herself once she sees the money. LaunchWitness never sees a bank and never claims a payment happened.

**Why no payment gateway?**
A gateway needs the seller's KYC, a business bank account and fees, which is a real barrier for a home seller who
already gets paid by UPI every day. UPI links move money straight from the customer to the seller; nothing passes
through LaunchWitness. Card payments through a gateway are listed as future work.

**Why hide the UPI ID on the shop page?**
A UPI ID on a public page can be copied onto a fake shop, and it invites payments with no order behind them. So the
shop page says how payment works but shows no ID or QR. The UPI details appear only after a real order, on the
thank-you page and the order's own unguessable status page, with the exact amount and the order reference.

**What if Claude is wrong, or someone hides instructions in their shop description?**
Claude never acts. It returns data (a profile, names, a finding, a fix id, OK or hold), and code validates every
field. The Doctor can only pick from five fixes written in code; anything else is refused and logged. The seller's
text and every tool result are passed to Claude as data, and a prompt-injection seller is part of the test suite.
The Reader's output is shown to the seller on Review before anything goes live. The policy check can only hold a shop
for a human; it can never launch one.

**What if the Claude API is down or over budget?**
Every call has a tight `max_tokens` and there is a daily spend cap. When Claude can't answer: the policy check fails
closed (the shop is held for the team, not launched), the Doctor falls back to plain rules (a single allowed standard
fix, or clear instructions for the owner), and the Reader shows a plain message asking the seller to try again.
Checks, repairs and monitoring are plain code and keep working.

**What does it cost to run?**
One GoDaddy VPS, the `launchwitness.com` domain and one GoDaddy Professional Email mailbox, all from hackathon credit;
real shops use free subdomains, so no domain is bought per seller. Claude is a few calls per launch: the Reader
(strong model) once, the Namer and the policy check (cheap model) once each, and the Doctor only when a check fails.
The live Claude spend is capped per day in configuration.

**How do custom orders work?**
An item can be marked "Takes custom requests" (photo cakes, theme cakes, tailoring, custom gifts). The Reader sets
it only when the seller's own words say so, and she can switch it on Review. When a customer orders such an item, the
form asks "Tell us what you want" for it (up to 500 characters: the message on the cake, the design, measurements)
and allows one reference photo (JPG, PNG or WebP, up to 5 MB). The photo is re-drawn from its pixels (no location or
camera data), is visible only to the seller on her Orders page, is never attached to an email or given a public
link, and is deleted 30 days after the order is done or cancelled.

**Isn't it one template?**
Yes, on purpose: one rendering engine and one template, server-rendered. That is what makes every shop testable and
safe (strict CSP, escaping tested in every look, the checker's marker on every page). Within it there are six looks
for home businesses (bakery, home kitchen, handmade, tailoring, gifts, general), each with accent colours, its own
fonts and a per-shop drawn signature, plus the seller's own photos. Claude picks keys; code draws everything.

# LaunchWitness: from description to a proven, live business

*GoDaddy Inclusive Innovation Hackathon 2026 · Open Innovation · one-page brief (draft for the PDF)*

> **Describe your business. LaunchWitness launches it on GoDaddy and proves everything works before your first customer arrives.**

## Problem

Small sellers like Meera, who bakes cakes at home and takes orders in Instagram messages, either never get online or end up with a setup that is quietly broken.
- **Setup is technical.** A GoDaddy survey found 63% of India's small businesses had no website. Of those planning one, 30% wanted someone to build and manage it for them. *(Older survey: background only. A 2025–26 figure is still to find.)*
- **Half-working setups go unnoticed.** Only 44.9% of small businesses use DMARC, against 75.3% of large enterprises (March 2026). In a scan of small-business domains, 36% had no SPF record. The result is that order emails land in spam, and the owner just thinks business is slow.
- **AI could do the setup, but isn't trusted to.** It means spending money and changing email settings for someone who can't check the work.

## Solution

Meera types two lines and pastes her price list.
- **Reader:** LaunchWitness builds her mobile site (menu in ₹, WhatsApp button, UPI QR, order form).
- **Namer:** it suggests real, available domain names with their prices.
- **Approval card:** one card shows every step, every setting as before and after, and the exact cost. Nothing happens until she approves.

Then it **launches and proves**. It points the domain, sets up her business email and turns on HTTPS. Then it checks every part for real: the address, the HTTPS certificate, the four email settings, and **a real test order arriving in her inbox**. A failed check is explained in one plain sentence ("Order emails could land in spam: a protection setting is missing"), fixed from a safe playbook, and re-checked to green.

The report says **"Your business is ready for customers"**, with the time each check passed. After launch it keeps watching:
- every 15 minutes: the site and HTTPS
- daily: the email settings and the days left on the domain and certificate

Warnings go to her personal email.

## How GoDaddy is used

GoDaddy is the engine, not decoration:
- **Domains:** availability and price for the suggested names. Purchase stays with the owner on godaddy.com and is adopted after her approval.
- **DNS API:**
  - a backup of the zone before any change
  - scoped record writes (A, MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC)
  - undo from the backup
  - checks asked of GoDaddy's authoritative nameservers
- **Email (Titan):** creates or adopts the business mailbox, then sends and receives orders through `smtpout.secureserver.net` / IMAP.
- **Docker VPS:** hosts everything. Caddy issues HTTPS for every seller site on demand, but only for domains in the app's database.

Sandbox launches use free subdomains of the app's own domain, so judges can try the real flow without buying anything.

## How Claude is used

Claude **decides and explains**; code **acts and checks**. There are three Claude roles:
- **Reader** (strong model, 1 call): description, price list or photo → a strict profile schema.
- **Namer** (cheap model): suggests about 10 names, which code then checks.
- **Doctor** (cheap model): one plain sentence for a failed check, plus a fix id. The fix must come from a fixed playbook, and code applies it.

A launch costs about 3 calls plus 1 per failed check, with `max_tokens` limits and a daily spend cap. The whole product was also **built with Claude Code** in recorded sessions. A planned, tested and documented session ritual is replayed at `/build`, with a summary of each session in `BUILD_LOG.md`.

## Safety

- **Approve before spending.** Purchases are off by default, have a hard spend cap and need the owner's approval record.
- **Preview before changing.** Every DNS change is shown as before and after.
- **Back up, then undo.** Writes without a backup are refused.
- **Scoped actions.** A launch only touches its own domain, one record at a time. The Doctor can't act outside its 5-fix playbook (max 3 attempts, never spends money); anything else is refused and logged.
- **Full audit log** in every report.
- **Safe public link:** practice mode for visitors, per-visitor limits, a secret owner link per business, and no secrets in the repo.

## What's next

1. Go live on the GoDaddy VPS and app domain; launch Meera's real domain on camera.
2. Full monitoring: a daily real test order, and change detection ("Was this you? Tap to restore") instead of silent fixes.
3. A `/verify` page backed by a DNS TXT record, so buyers can spot fake shops using her name.
4. Run on the seller's own GoDaddy account, where monitoring matters most.
5. More languages for the description, and a template per trade (food, tailoring, tuition).

# HackerEarth submission: values to paste

## Title

LaunchWitness: from business idea to customer-ready, proven on GoDaddy

## Theme

Open Innovation

## Demo link

https://launchwitness.com

## Repository URL

https://github.com/aarushitandon0/LaunchWitness

> Note for the owner: this repository is private today (it answers 404 when signed out). Make it public, or add the
> judges as collaborators, before submitting; otherwise rely on the Source Code zip.

## Files

- **Source Code:** `dist/LaunchWitness-source.zip` (a `git archive` of the final `main` commit: tracked files only)
- **Additional File:** `dist/LaunchWitness-brief.pdf` (the project brief)

## Description (Markdown)

**From business idea to customer-ready. Be ready before your first customer arrives.**

Home sellers in India (cakes, tiffins, tailoring, gift hampers) take orders over Instagram and WhatsApp. When they do
get a website, nobody checks it works end to end: a missing email setting sends orders to spam, an address stops
pointing at the shop, and the seller just sees fewer orders.

**LaunchWitness** builds a seller's shop from a few lines and her price list, launches it on GoDaddy, and then
**proves a real order reaches her**: it places a test order through the shop's own public form and follows it until
it is found in the inbox. It also checks the address (on GoDaddy's own nameservers), HTTPS and email settings, fixes
what fails from a fixed playbook of safe repairs, and keeps checking after launch. The report says "ready for
customers" only when every check passed, and every claim sits in a tamper-evident evidence chain anyone can
re-verify.

**Claude decides and explains; plain code acts.** Claude reads her messy menu (Reader), suggests names (Namer),
explains a failed check and picks a fix from the playbook (Doctor), and can hold a shop for review (policy check). It
never spends money or writes DNS: code does, with backups, spend guards and an audit row for every change.

**GoDaddy is load-bearing:** the domain, DNS writes through the GoDaddy API (backed up first), a GoDaddy VPS running
Docker with automatic HTTPS, and a GoDaddy Professional Email mailbox for SMTP sending and IMAP proof.

For customers: prices in ₹ with sizes, pickup or delivery, UPI shown only after an order ("Customer says paid" for the
seller to check), and custom requests with a reference photo for photo cakes and tailoring.

**Links**
- App: https://launchwitness.com
- A real launched shop: https://meeras-eggless-bakes.launchwitness.com
- Its proof report: https://launchwitness.com/r/GsZj7gOAoCydSauqdNpoaWksKHVW-HSz (add `/verify` to recompute the chain)
- How it was built with Claude Code: https://launchwitness.com/build

**Try it with no account:** open the app → **Try it without an account** → pick an example seller → run a practice
launch (everything runs against a pretend GoDaddy; nothing is bought). Or open a demo shop, e.g.
https://launchwitness.com/demo/meera.
