  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
    - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, .claude/settings.local.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice.

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

severity.description: Set when the review instructions ask for it. important: a bug the change adds or makes worse; pre_existing: a bug that was there before the change; nit: a minor issue

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

content.text: Tool loaded.

lastPrompt: Session 22 (LAPTOP, FINAL). Submission TODAY 10 PM IST. HARD CUT-OFF for deploying features: 6:30 PM IST. After 6:30: docs + submission files only. Never spend money or touch DNS without asking me. Re…

LaunchWitness

From business idea to customer-ready.
Be ready before your first customer arrives.

Submission for the GoDaddy Inclusive Innovation Hackathon 2026 (Round 2, Open Innovation)

LaunchWitness builds a home seller's online shop, puts it online on GoDaddy, **places a real test order through the shop's own order form and proves it reaches the seller's inbox**, fixes what breaks from a fixed list of safe repairs, and keeps checking after launch. ## Live links | What | Link | |---|---| | The app | https://launchwitness.com | | A real shop launched by the app (Meera's demo bakery) | https://meeras-eggless-bakes.launchwitness.com | | A demo shop (sample, orders are not real) | https://launchwitness.com/demo/meera | | That shop's shared proof report | https://launchwitness.com/r/GsZj7gOAoCydSauqdNpoaWksKHVW-HSz | | Recompute the report's evidence chain yourself | https://launchwitness.com/r/GsZj7gOAoCydSauqdNpoaWksKHVW-HSz/verify | | How it was built with Claude Code (session replay) | https://launchwitness.com/build | **Trying it as a judge, no account needed:** open https://launchwitness.com, press **Try it without an account**, pick an example seller, review the shop, and run a **practice launch**. Practice mode runs every step against a pretend GoDaddy: nothing is bought and nothing goes on the internet. Then open the eight demo shops from the strip on the landing page (`/demo/meera`, `/demo/imran`, `/demo/sunita`, ...). --- ## The problem Many home sellers in India (cakes, tiffins, tailoring, crafts, gift hampers) take orders in Instagram and WhatsApp messages. When they do get a website, nobody checks that it actually works end to end. A missing email setting sends order emails to spam; a form posts to nowhere; an address stops pointing at the shop. The seller sees no error message. She just gets fewer orders and thinks business is slow. Our demo persona is **Meera**, who bakes eggless cakes at home in Pune. She doesn't know what DNS is, and she shouldn't have to. What she needs to know is one thing: **if a customer orders, will I get it?** --- ## How it works, in five steps | # | Step | Who does it | What happens | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | **Describe** | Seller + Claude | She types a few lines and pastes her price list (or uploads a photo of it, even handwritten). Claude reads it into a structured shop: items and prices in ₹, sizes, notice needed, pickup or delivery, hours, area. | | 2 | **Review** | Seller | The shop appears as an ordinary form and a private preview. She fixes anything wrong, adds photos, picks one of six looks, and marks items that take custom requests. No AI involved. | | 3 | **Launch on GoDaddy** | Code only, after she approves | One approval card shows every step, every setting as before → after, and the cost. On approval, code backs up the DNS records, writes the shop's record through the GoDaddy API, and the server issues HTTPS for the shop. | | 4 | **Prove a real order reaches her** | Code | The checker opens her public shop page, fills in the real order form like a customer, and follows that order: form accepted → mail server accepted → **found in the inbox** (read over IMAP) or **confirmed by her** ("Yes, I got it" link in the test email). It also checks the address, HTTPS and the email settings. The report says "ready for customers" only when every check passed. | | 5 | **Fix and keep watching** | Claude explains, code fixes | A failed check is explained in one plain sentence and repaired from a playbook of five fixes in code, then checked again. After launch the shop is re-checked every 15 minutes (site, HTTPS) and daily (settings, expiry dates, a test order to LaunchWitness's own check mailbox). Problems are emailed to her personal address. | After launch she also gets an **Orders** page (New → Confirmed → Paid → Done / Cancelled) and an email for every order. --- ## What Claude does, and what plain code does The rule: **Claude decides and explains; plain code acts and checks.** Claude never spends money and never writes DNS. | Claude (judgment) | Model | Job | |---|---|---| | **Reader** | Strong (`claude-sonnet-5-5`) | Turns her messy description and price list (text or photo, English or Hinglish) into a strict shop profile, its wording and its look. Code validates and tidies every field. | | **Namer** | Cheap (`claude-haiku-5-5`) | Suggests about ten shop names. Code checks which are available and what they cost. | | **Doctor / Investigator** | Cheap | Looks at a failed check with read-only tools (look up the shop's own address, fetch its own page, read stored evidence, test the mail server sign-in without sending), then explains it in one sentence and picks a fix id from the playbook, or says "needs you". | | **Policy check** | Cheap | Is this shop OK to put live? It can only **hold** a shop for a human to look at. It can never launch or unpause one. | | Plain code (guarded, audited) | Job | |---|---| | **Money** | A purchase needs all three: `ALLOW_PURCHASE=true` (off by default), a cost under `MAX_SPEND_USD`, and the owner's approval record. In this build the app never bought anything. | | **DNS** | Planner shows every change as before → after; Executor backs up first, writes only to domains in the app's own database, one record at a time, and can undo from the backup. | | **Rendering** | One template draws every shop, server-side. Claude only picks keys (which look, which accent); code draws everything. | | **Checks** | The Checker proves each claim and stores it as evidence. The Doctor's chosen fix is applied by code, and only if it is in the playbook and allowed for that check. | Every state change writes an audit row (who, what, when, result). If Claude is unavailable or over its daily budget, plain rules take over: the launch check holds, and the Doctor falls back to a standard fix or clear instructions. --- ## How GoDaddy is load-bearing | GoDaddy product | What LaunchWitness does with it | |---|---| | **Domain** | `launchwitness.com` is registered at GoDaddy. Every real shop lives at `.launchwitness.com`. | | **DNS API** | At launch the app backs up the zone's records, then writes one A record for the shop through the GoDaddy API (guarded client, scoped to its own records). The demo shop's record was written this way. Undo restores from the backup. | | **Authoritative nameservers** | The address check asks GoDaddy's own nameservers, not a cache, so the answer is the real one. | | **VPS (Docker)** | One GoDaddy VPS runs everything with Docker Compose: Caddy (HTTPS for the app and an on-demand certificate for each shop, only for shops in the database) and the FastAPI app. | | **Professional Email (Titan) mailbox** | `hello@launchwitness.com`. The app sends every email (sign-in links, order emails, test orders, the contact form) over **SMTP** (`smtpout.secureserver.net`), and reads the inbox over **IMAP** to prove a test order arrived. | | **HTTPS** | Let's Encrypt certificates through Caddy, for the apex, `www` and each shop subdomain. | --- ## Hackathon requirements: how to verify each one | Requirement | Where | How to check it | |---|---|---| | Live app hosted on GoDaddy | GoDaddy VPS | Open https://launchwitness.com | | Own domain over HTTPS | `launchwitness.com` (GoDaddy) | The padlock on https://launchwitness.com and https://meeras-eggless-bakes.launchwitness.com | | A mailbox that receives a test email | `hello@launchwitness.com` (GoDaddy Professional Email) | The shared report's test-order row: "found in the inbox" with the time, read over IMAP | | Contact form delivers to the mailbox via SMTP | Landing page, "Contact us" | `backend/app/routers/contact.py` sends to `SMTP_USER` through the SMTP mailer; each message is audited | | No password in code or repo | `.env` exists only on the server | `bash scripts/secret_scan.sh` scans the repo and the whole git history; `.env.example` has no values | --- ## Safety - **Strict Content-Security-Policy on every shop page.** Scripts run only if their hash matches the template's own fixed scripts, so a script that came from a seller's words could never run. - **Escaping, tested.** Every seller-supplied and customer-supplied field is HTML-escaped. Tests put a hostile string into every field, in every one of the six looks, and in the order email. - **Private UPI.** A shop page never shows the seller's UPI ID or QR code. Only after a real order does the thank-you page (and the order's own private status page) show a UPI link and QR for the exact amount. A customer can then say "I've paid" with the 12-digit UPI reference and an optional screenshot. The seller sees **"Customer says paid"**, never "Paid": she checks her own UPI app first. - **Held edits.** When a live shop's owner changes its words, the policy check runs again; if it isn't sure, the edit waits for the team and the shop stays live as it was. - **Spend caps.** Purchases are off by default and capped; Claude has a daily spend cap; every Claude call has a tight `max_tokens`. - **Tamper-evident evidence.** Every claim on a report comes from a stored evidence row. Each shop's rows form an append-only hash chain. Anyone with the report link can open `/verify` and the server recomputes the chain: "Intact", or exactly which row changed. - **Uploads.** Product photos, payment screenshots and custom-order reference photos all go through one gate: size cap, content sniff (JPEG, PNG or WebP by what the file is, not its name), pixel cap, then a brand-new image is drawn from the pixels alone, so no location or camera data survives. Screenshots and reference photos are owner-only and deleted 30 days after the order is done or cancelled. - **The checker can't be pointed at private addresses.** It reaches websites only through an SSRF guard (private, loopback and cloud-metadata addresses refused, IP pinned, every redirect re-checked). More in [`docs/SECURITY.md`](docs/SECURITY.md). --- ## Custom orders Photo cakes, theme cakes, tailoring and custom gifts need the seller to **see** what the customer wants before she accepts. An item can be marked **"Takes custom requests"** (the Reader sets it only from the seller's own words, such as "photo cake" or "stitching"; she can switch it on Review). When a customer's basket has such an item, the order form asks "Tell us what you want" for that item (up to 500 characters) and allows **one** reference photo (JPG, PNG or WebP, up to 5 MB). The seller sees both on her Orders page. The order email carries the notes and says "Reference photo: open it in Orders"; the photo is never attached and never has a public link. --- ## What's real today, and what is practice mode **Real, running in production on the GoDaddy VPS** - The app at https://launchwitness.com with Let's Encrypt HTTPS. - One real shop launched by the app: Meera's demo bakery. Its DNS record was written through the GoDaddy API with a backup first, its certificate was issued on demand, and its shared report shows every check proven with an intact evidence chain. - Real email through GoDaddy Professional Email: sign-in links, order emails, test orders (found in the inbox over IMAP) and the contact form. - Monitoring, nightly database backups with a tested restore. - Live Claude calls for the Reader, Namer, Doctor and policy check, under a daily spend cap. **Practice mode (clearly labelled "Practice" everywhere)** - Guests and new accounts launch in practice mode: the same code runs against in-memory fakes of GoDaddy, DNS, the mailbox and HTTPS. Nothing is bought and nothing goes on the internet. - The eight `/demo/*` shops are samples: their order form places no order and stores nothing, and their WhatsApp button opens a page that says it is a demo. **Not done yet** - **Launches on a seller's own domain** were cut for this round. They work in practice mode; real launches use a free `.launchwitness.com` address. No domain was bought by the app. - **Creating a mailbox per seller** through GoDaddy's email API is still a stub. Order emails go to the seller's verified sign-in email. - **Payments** are UPI links only. No money passes through LaunchWitness, so it never confirms a payment. - **The demo fault switch** (for showing the Doctor on camera) stages a fault; detecting and repairing it is real code. - **The admin** is whoever controls the admin email inbox; there is no second factor yet. --- ## Tech stack | Layer | Technology | |---|---| | Backend | Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLModel + SQLite (WAL), httpx, dnspython, APScheduler, Jinja2, Pillow, `anthropic` SDK | | Frontend | React + Vite + TypeScript, plain CSS | | Seller shops | Server-rendered Jinja2, one template, six looks, self-hosted open-licence fonts | | Infrastructure | GoDaddy VPS, Docker Compose, Caddy (automatic HTTPS, on-demand TLS) | | Email | GoDaddy Professional Email over SMTP and IMAP; Mailpit for the local stack | | Tests | pytest, Playwright, ruff | --- ## Run it locally Practice mode needs no keys: fakes for every outside service and saved Claude responses. ```bash cp .env.example .env # safe defaults: fakes on, sandbox, purchases off python3.12 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/pip install -r backend/requirements-dev.txt (cd frontend && npm install && npm run build) cd backend && ../.venv/bin/uvicorn app.main:app --port 8000 # http://localhost:8000 ``` Set `DEV_MODE=true` in `.env` so sign-in links show on screen instead of being emailed. On Windows use `.venv/Scripts/python -m uvicorn ...`. A production-like stack (HTTPS through Caddy's local CA, fakes, Mailpit at http://localhost:8025): ```bash docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml \ -f deploy/docker-compose.local.yml up -d --build --wait # https://launchwitness.localhost bash scripts/check_m1.sh --local ``` Production on the VPS: [`docs/RUNBOOK_M1.md`](docs/RUNBOOK_M1.md) and [`docs/NEXT_SESSION_VPS.md`](docs/NEXT_SESSION_VPS.md). --- ## Tests ```bash cd backend && ../.venv/bin/pytest -q # tests block every real network call .venv/bin/python -m ruff check backend cd frontend && npx tsc --noEmit && npm run build cd e2e && npm install && npx playwright install chromium && npx playwright test # against the Docker stack bash scripts/secret_scan.sh ``` Results from the final session's runs (20 Nov 2026): TEST_COUNTS_PLACEHOLDER What they cover, among other things: every check scenario in [`docs/CHECKS_MATRIX.md`](docs/CHECKS_MATRIX.md); access control for every route (a test fails if a route is missing from the route table); hostile input in every field in every look; SSRF; the spend and DNS guards; the Claude agents against saved real responses, including a prompt-injection seller and a handwritten price-list photo; and browser flows from describing a shop to a customer's order arriving on the Orders page. --- ## Screenshots | | | |---|---| | Landing page (1440 px) ![Landing](docs/screenshots/s22/hero-1440.png) | Meera's live shop on a phone ![Live shop](docs/screenshots/s20b/live-demo-shop-390.png) | | The proof report ![Report](docs/screenshots/s12/10-report-1440.png) | The seller's Orders page ![Orders](docs/screenshots/s10-5/07-orders-page-1440.png) | All six shop looks: [`docs/screenshots/s14/contact-sheet.png`](docs/screenshots/s14/contact-sheet.png). --- ## Built with Claude Code The whole product was built in Claude Code, in recorded sessions that followed one written ritual ([`CLAUDE.md`](CLAUDE.md)): read the progress file, propose a plan against the acceptance criteria in [`docs/BUILD_PLAN.md`](docs/BUILD_PLAN.md), make small tested commits, update [`docs/PROGRESS.md`](docs/PROGRESS.md) and [`docs/BUILD_LOG.md`](docs/BUILD_LOG.md), and save a redacted, secret-scanned transcript. Product decisions stayed with the human. Claude reads it into a structured shop: items and prices in ₹, sizes, notice needed, pickup or delivery, hours, area. | | 2 | **Review** | Seller | The shop appears as an ordinary form and a private preview. She fixes anything wrong, adds photos, picks one of six looks, and marks items that take custom requests. No AI involved. | | 3 | **Launch on GoDaddy** | Code only, after she approves | One approval card shows every step, every setting as before → after, and the cost. Code validates and tidies every field. | | **Namer** | Cheap (`claude-haiku-5-5`) | Suggests about ten shop names. lines: -**Isn't this just a website builder, or GoDaddy Airo?**
-No. Building the shop is step one of five, and the least new one. What LaunchWitness adds is the part no builder
-does: after the shop goes live, it places a real test order through the shop's own public order form and follows it
-until it is found in the inbox (or the seller taps "Yes, I got it"). It checks the address, HTTPS and email settings,
-repairs what fails from a fixed playbook, and keeps checking after launch. The report only says "ready for customers"
-when every check has passed, and each claim is backed by stored, tamper-evident evidence.
-**How does the seller know a customer paid?**
-She checks her own UPI app. After a real order the customer sees a UPI link and QR code for the exact amount, with
-the order reference as the payment note. After paying, the customer can enter the 12-digit UPI reference (and an
-optional screenshot). The seller's Orders page then shows **"Customer says paid"**, never "Paid". She marks the order
-Paid herself once she sees the money. LaunchWitness never sees a bank and never claims a payment happened.
-A gateway needs the seller's KYC, a business bank account and fees, which is a real barrier for a home seller who
-already gets paid by UPI every day. UPI links move money straight from the customer to the seller; nothing passes
-through LaunchWitness. Card payments through a gateway are listed as future work.
-**Why hide the UPI ID on the shop page?**
-A UPI ID on a public page can be copied onto a fake shop, and it invites payments with no order behind them. So the
-shop page says how payment works but shows no ID or QR. The UPI details appear only after a real order, on the
-thank-you page and the order's own unguessable status page, with the exact amount and the order reference.
-**What if Claude is wrong, or someone hides instructions in their shop description?**
-Claude never acts. It returns data (a profile, names, a finding, a fix id, OK or hold), and code validates every
-field. The Doctor can only pick from five fixes written in code; anything else is refused and logged. The seller's
-text and every tool result are passed to Claude as data, and a prompt-injection seller is part of the test suite.
-The Reader's output is shown to the seller on Review before anything goes live. The policy check can only hold a shop
-for a human; it can never launch one.
-**What if the Claude API is down or over budget?**
-Every call has a tight `max_tokens` and there is a daily spend cap. When Claude can't answer: the policy check fails
-closed (the shop is held for the team, not launched), the Doctor falls back to plain rules (a single allowed standard
-fix, or clear instructions for the owner), and the Reader shows a plain message asking the seller to try again.
-Checks, repairs and monitoring are plain code and keep working.
-One GoDaddy VPS, the `launchwitness.com` domain and one GoDaddy Professional Email mailbox, all from hackathon credit;
-real shops use free subdomains, so no domain is bought per seller. Claude is a few calls per launch: the Reader
-(strong model) once, the Namer and the policy check (cheap model) once each, and the Doctor only when a check fails.
-The live Claude spend is capped per day in configuration.
-An item can be marked "Takes custom requests" (photo cakes, theme cakes, tailoring, custom gifts). The Reader sets
-it only when the seller's own words say so, and she can switch it on Review. When a customer orders such an item, the
-form asks "Tell us what you want" for it (up to 500 characters: the message on the cake, the design, measurements)
-and allows one reference photo (JPG, PNG or WebP, up to 5 MB). The photo is re-drawn from its pixels (no location or
-camera data), is visible only to the seller on her Orders page, is never attached to an email or given a public
-link, and is deleted 30 days after the order is done or cancelled.
-Yes, on purpose: one rendering engine and one template, server-rendered. That is what makes every shop testable and
-safe (strict CSP, escaping tested in every look, the checker's marker on every page). Within it there are six looks
-for home businesses (bakery, home kitchen, handmade, tailoring, gifts, general), each with accent colours, its own
-fonts and a per-shop drawn signature, plus the seller's own photos. Claude picks keys; code draws everything.

+# LaunchWitness: from description to a proven, live business
+*GoDaddy Inclusive Innovation Hackathon 2026 · Open Innovation · one-page brief (draft for the PDF)*
+> **Describe your business. LaunchWitness launches it on GoDaddy and proves everything works before your first customer arrives.**
+Small sellers like Meera, who bakes cakes at home and takes orders in Instagram messages, either never get online or end up with a setup that is quietly broken.

+- **Setup is technical.** A GoDaddy survey found 63% of India's small businesses had no website. Of those planning one, 30% wanted someone to build and manage it for them. *(Older survey: background only. A 2025–26 figure is still to find.)*

+- **Half-working setups go unnoticed.** Only 44.9% of small businesses use DMARC, against 75.3% of large enterprises (March 2026). In a scan of small-business domains, 36% had no SPF record. The result is that order emails land in spam, and the owner just thinks business is slow.
+- **AI could do the setup, but isn't trusted to.** It means spending money and changing email settings for someone who can't check the work.
+Meera types two lines and pastes her price list.
+- **Reader:** LaunchWitness builds her mobile site (menu in ₹, WhatsApp button, UPI QR, order form).
+- **Namer:** it suggests real, available domain names with their prices.
+- **Approval card:** one card shows every step, every setting as before and after, and the exact cost. Nothing happens until she approves.

+Then it **launches and proves**. It points the domain, sets up her business email and turns on HTTPS. Then it checks every part for real: the address, the HTTPS certificate, the four email settings, and **a real test order arriving in her inbox**. A failed check is explained in one plain sentence ("Order emails could land in spam: a protection setting is missing"), fixed from a safe playbook, and re-checked to green.
+The report says **"Your business is ready for customers"**, with the time each check passed. After launch it keeps watching:
+- every 15 minutes: the site and HTTPS
+- daily: the email settings and the days left on the domain and certificate
+- **Domains:** availability and price for the suggested names. Purchase stays with the owner on godaddy.com and is adopted after her approval.
+  - a backup of the zone before any change
+  - scoped record writes (A, MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC)
+  - checks asked of GoDaddy's authoritative nameservers
+- **Email (Titan):** creates or adopts the business mailbox, then sends and receives orders through `smtpout.secureserver.net` / IMAP.
+- **Docker VPS:** hosts everything. Caddy issues HTTPS for every seller site on demand, but only for domains in the app's database.
+Sandbox launches use free subdomains of the app's own domain, so judges can try the real flow without buying anything.
+Claude **decides and explains**; code **acts and checks**. There are three Claude roles:
+- **Reader** (strong model, 1 call): description, price list or photo → a strict profile schema.
+- **Namer** (cheap model): suggests about 10 names, which code then checks.
+- **Doctor** (cheap model): one plain sentence for a failed check, plus a fix id. The fix must come from a fixed playbook, and code applies it.

+A launch costs about 3 calls plus 1 per failed check, with `max_tokens` limits and a daily spend cap. The whole product was also **built with Claude Code** in recorded sessions. A planned, tested and documented session ritual is replayed at `/build`, with a summary of each session in `BUILD_LOG.md`.
+- **Approve before spending.** Purchases are off by default, have a hard spend cap and need the owner's approval record.
+- **Preview before changing.** Every DNS change is shown as before and after.
+- **Back up, then undo.** Writes without a backup are refused.

+- **Scoped actions.** A launch only touches its own domain, one record at a time. The Doctor can't act outside its 5-fix playbook (max 3 attempts, never spends money); anything else is refused and logged.
+- **Safe public link:** practice mode for visitors, per-visitor limits, a secret owner link per business, and no secrets in the repo.
+1. Go live on the GoDaddy VPS and app domain; launch Meera's real domain on camera.
+2. Full monitoring: a daily real test order, and change detection ("Was this you? Tap to restore") instead of silent fixes.
+3. A `/verify` page backed by a DNS TXT record, so buyers can spot fake shops using her name.
+4. Run on the seller's own GoDaddy account, where monitoring matters most.
+5. More languages for the description, and a template per trade (food, tailoring, tuition).

lines: +**Isn't this just a website builder, or GoDaddy Airo?**
+No. Building the shop is step one of five, and the least new one. What LaunchWitness adds is the part no builder
+does: after the shop goes live, it places a real test order through the shop's own public order form and follows it
+until it is found in the inbox (or the seller taps "Yes, I got it"). It checks the address, HTTPS and email settings,
+repairs what fails from a fixed playbook, and keeps checking after launch. The report only says "ready for customers"
+when every check has passed, and each claim is backed by stored, tamper-evident evidence.
+**How does the seller know a customer paid?**
+She checks her own UPI app. After a real order the customer sees a UPI link and QR code for the exact amount, with
+the order reference as the payment note. After paying, the customer can enter the 12-digit UPI reference (and an
+optional screenshot). The seller's Orders page then shows **"Customer says paid"**, never "Paid". She marks the order
+Paid herself once she sees the money. LaunchWitness never sees a bank and never claims a payment happened.
+A gateway needs the seller's KYC, a business bank account and fees, which is a real barrier for a home seller who
+already gets paid by UPI every day. UPI links move money straight from the customer to the seller; nothing passes
+through LaunchWitness. Card payments through a gateway are listed as future work.
+**Why hide the UPI ID on the shop page?**
+A UPI ID on a public page can be copied onto a fake shop, and it invites payments with no order behind them. So the
+shop page says how payment works but shows no ID or QR. The UPI details appear only after a real order, on the
+thank-you page and the order's own unguessable status page, with the exact amount and the order reference.
+**What if Claude is wrong, or someone hides instructions in their shop description?**
+Claude never acts. It returns data (a profile, names, a finding, a fix id, OK or hold), and code validates every
+field. The Doctor can only pick from five fixes written in code; anything else is refused and logged. The seller's
+text and every tool result are passed to Claude as data, and a prompt-injection seller is part of the test suite.
+The Reader's output is shown to the seller on Review before anything goes live. The policy check can only hold a shop
+for a human; it can never launch one.
+**What if the Claude API is down or over budget?**
+Every call has a tight `max_tokens` and there is a daily spend cap. When Claude can't answer: the policy check fails
+closed (the shop is held for the team, not launched), the Doctor falls back to plain rules (a single allowed standard
+fix, or clear instructions for the owner), and the Reader shows a plain message asking the seller to try again.
+Checks, repairs and monitoring are plain code and keep working.
+One GoDaddy VPS, the `launchwitness.com` domain and one GoDaddy Professional Email mailbox, all from hackathon credit;
+real shops use free subdomains, so no domain is bought per seller. Claude is a few calls per launch: the Reader
+(strong model) once, the Namer and the policy check (cheap model) once each, and the Doctor only when a check fails.
+The live Claude spend is capped per day in configuration.
+An item can be marked "Takes custom requests" (photo cakes, theme cakes, tailoring, custom gifts). The Reader sets
+it only when the seller's own words say so, and she can switch it on Review. When a customer orders such an item, the
+form asks "Tell us what you want" for it (up to 500 characters: the message on the cake, the design, measurements)
+and allows one reference photo (JPG, PNG or WebP, up to 5 MB). The photo is re-drawn from its pixels (no location or
+camera data), is visible only to the seller on her Orders page, is never attached to an email or given a public
+link, and is deleted 30 days after the order is done or cancelled.
+Yes, on purpose: one rendering engine and one template, server-rendered. That is what makes every shop testable and
+safe (strict CSP, escaping tested in every look, the checker's marker on every page). Within it there are six looks
+for home businesses (bakery, home kitchen, handmade, tailoring, gifts, general), each with accent colours, its own
+fonts and a per-shop drawn signature, plus the seller's own photos. Claude picks keys; code draws everything.
